summary: This is a House class that stores an address, a bedroom count, and a bathroom count, with getters and setters for each. It also overrides toString so that printing a House produces a readable line of text describing it.

lines.text: The address is declared private so that outside code cannot reach in and change it directly; access goes through the methods below instead.
Bathrooms is a double rather than an int because half-baths are real: a house can have 2.5 bathrooms.

lines.code: public House(String address, int bedrooms, double bathrooms) {
lines.text: The constructor runs when a House is created with new, and it demands all three values up front so no House ever exists in a half-filled state.
The parameter and the field share the name address, so this.address makes it clear that the field is on the left and the parameter is on the right.
A getter hands out the stored value on request, which is how private data is read from outside the class.
A setter is the single doorway for changing the address, which is where validation would go if the class ever needed to reject bad input.
This annotation tells the compiler you intend to replace a method inherited from Object; if the signature below does not match, you get an error instead of a silent bug.

Every object inherits toString from Object, and Java calls it automatically inside println or string concatenation. Overriding it replaces the useless default like House@1b6d3586 with something meaningful.
The returned string is assembled by concatenating literal text with the field values, spread over several lines purely for readability.
The single quotes wrap the address so an empty or space-padded value is still visible in the output; '\\'' is the escape sequence for a literal single-quote character.
The closing brace finishes the format, producing output such as House{address='12 Oak St', bedrooms=3, bathrooms=2.5}.
